desc:
Consider a path in a binary tree: a sequence of nodes in which every two neighbours are parent and child, and no node is repeated. The path may start and end anywhere and may turn at a node (go up to a common ancestor, then down). Call it consecutive if, read from one end to the other, the values change by exactly +1 at every step, or by exactly -1 at every step. The two directions must not be mixed: 1, 2, 1 is not consecutive. A single node is a consecutive path.

Return the number of nodes on the longest consecutive path (0 for the empty tree).

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [2, 1, 3] the answer is 3: the path 1 → 2 → 3 goes up from the left child through the root to the right child. For tree = [1, 2, 3] the answer is 2, since 2 → 1 → 3 mixes a decrease with an increase.
constraints: The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
hints: Look at the node where the path turns. The part of the path on each side of it is a downward chain.
For each node keep two numbers: the longest downward chain that increases by 1 at each step (inc) and the longest that decreases by 1 at each step (dec), counted in nodes.

A path through v that increases in one direction is a dec chain going down on one side joined to an inc chain going down on the other. Its length is inc[v] + dec[v] - 1. The two chains use different children automatically, because the child values are val[v] + 1 and val[v] - 1.
editorial: Every path has a highest node v (the turning point), and both parts of the path below it are downward chains. Suppose the whole path increases when read from left to right. The part ending at v read downward goes v, v-1, v-2, ..., a decreasing chain, and the part that continues from v goes v, v+1, v+2, ..., an increasing chain. The mirror image (path decreasing left to right) swaps the roles, so one formula covers both.

Compute for every node inc[v] = the number of nodes of the longest downward chain starting at v with each step +1, and dec[v] likewise with each step -1. Both are at least 1. For a child c: if val[c] = val[v] + 1 then inc[v] = max(inc[v], inc[c] + 1), and if val[c] = val[v] - 1 then dec[v] = max(dec[v], dec[c] + 1). A child cannot satisfy both, so the two chains at v never share a child.

The longest consecutive path that turns at v has inc[v] + dec[v] - 1 nodes (v is counted once). Take the maximum over all nodes. A backwards pass over the level-order array processes the children first: O(n) time and O(n) space.
